                           STACY RANDOLPH'S INITIAL BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

I. INTRODUCTION
    Intervenor Stacy Randolph respectfully submits this Initial Brief as Nelda Howton's
daughter, future heir of the Howton property, and a pro se intervenor whose family property and
future use of the land would be directly affected by any route using Link F-20. Ms. Randolph
opposes Route 894 and any other route using Link F-20 because that link would place
unnecessary and concentrated impacts on her parents' residence, agricultural operations,
livestock uses, rural property, community values, safety, wildfire risk, storm recovery, cultural
resources, aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.
   The Cedar Valley community includes Cedar Valley Church, homes, farms, Buttermilk
Creek, livestock operations, and rural gathering places with cultural and historical meaning.
Cedar Valley Church serves as a community and disaster gathering place. Buttermilk Creek is
associated with the Gault archeological area and should be treated as a serious cultural-resource
concern.
    Ms. Randolph asks the Administrative Law Judges to recommend rejection of Route 894 and
any route using Link F-20, and to recommend Preferred Route 296 or another route that avoids
Link F-20 and better satisfies the statutory routing criteria. This brief summarizes and applies the
evidence already presented through her testimony and the Howton family evidence.

II. SUMMARY OF POSITION
   The question is not simply whether a transmission line is needed somewhere. The question is
whether the Applicants fairly applied the statutory routing criteria to the people, property, and
community resources that would bear the burden of a 765-kV transmission line.
   Link F-20 would place that burden too close to the Howton residence and agricultural
improvements. The property is used as a home and for cattle, horses, poultry, gardening, hunting,
and family outdoor activities. The record also raises concerns about visual impact, noise,
property use, wildfire risk, emergency access, storm vulnerability, cultural resources, and
cumulative infrastructure burdens.
   For these reasons, Ms. Randolph asks the ALJs to recommend Preferred Route 296 instead of
Route 894 or any other route using Link F-20. If the ALJs compare F-20 and F-21, the evidence
supports finding that F-21 is less harmful because it avoids or reduces the concentrated


                                                 1
 residential, church, cultural-resource, storm-recovery, and cumulative-infrastructure impacts
associated with F-20.

III. APPLICABLE LEGAL STANDARD
    Under PURA Section 37.056(c), the Commission must consider statutory factors relevant to
need and proper routing. PURA Section 37.056(c)(4) requires consideration of community
values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.
The Commission's routing criteria also consider use or paralleling of existing compatible rights-
of-way, other compatible rights-of-way, property lines, and natural or cultural features.
    Those factors should be applied to the facts in the record, including testimony from
landowners and family members who know the property, community, local hazards, land uses,
and cultural concerns. Ms. Randolph's testimony is offered from the perspective of Nelda
Howton's daughter and future heir, whose family property and future use of the land would be
affected.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Link F-20 would impose concentrated residential and property-use impacts on the
Howton family property.

    Ms. Randolph testified that the proposed line would be approximately 242 feet from the
centerline to her parents' residence and approximately 143 feet from the nearest transmission
structures and conductor locations, as reflected in the Howton aerial proximity evidence. Those
distances show a direct and close impact on the residence and daily use of the property.
    The Howton property is not vacant or unused. It includes a residence, barns, fencing, corrals,
livestock uses, and family outdoor activity on approximately 47 acres used for cattle, horses,
deer hunting, poultry, gardening, and general agricultural operations. Link F-20 would
substantially alter the rural character, use, and enjoyment of the property.
B. Link F-20 does not adequately protect community values.

    Community values include the rural residential character of the Cedar Valley/Salado area,
agricultural life, family use of land, Cedar Valley Church, recovery after the April 2022 tornado,
and the reasonable expectation that routing will not unnecessarily concentrate impacts on homes,
small rural landowners, and established community resources.
    The testimony and exhibits show that Link F-20 would burden an established rural property
and surrounding community features. The Applicants did not give sufficient weight to these
localized community values when comparing routes that include Link F-20 against available
alternatives.
C. Cedar Valley Church and Buttermilk Creek support avoiding Link F-20.

   Cedar Valley Church should be treated as more than a structure near a route. It is a
community meeting place and part of the Cedar Valley community's identity, disaster recovery,
and rural life. A 765-kV transmission line on Link F-20 would place a major industrial feature
near that community institution.
   Buttermilk Creek and the Gault archeological area raise important cultural-resource
concerns. A route affecting or crossing near Buttermilk Creek should receive careful scrutiny


                                                2
 under historical and aesthetic values and environmental integrity. An alternative link that avoids
or reduces those concerns should be given meaningful weight.
D. Tornado recovery supports avoiding additional infrastructure burdens in this area.

   The evidence includes storm and tornado-related materials documenting severe weather
damage, regional recovery, and property vulnerability. The Cedar Valley community has already
experienced significant tornado damage and remains affected by that recovery.
    A route that adds heavy infrastructure near a storm-damaged community should not be
preferred when a reasonable alternative, such as Preferred Route 296 or another non-F-20 route,
is available.
E. Agricultural, livestock, and family recreational uses support rejecting Link F-20.

   The Howton property supports livestock, equine activities, poultry, gardening, hunting, and
family outdoor use. These uses define the property and should be considered in the routing
decision.
   A 765-kV line could affect fencing, access, livestock behavior, property maintenance, family
outdoor use, and the continued practical use of the land. These concerns support rejection of
Link F-20.
F. Wildfire, vegetation, endangered-species, and emergency-response concerns support
rejecting Link F-20.

    The evidence identifies heavy vegetation, dry grass, cedar debris, and other conditions that
increase wildfire risk. It also raises environmental and habitat concerns associated with Link
F-20.
   A 765-kV line should not be routed in a manner that unnecessarily increases wildfire and
emergency-access concerns for a rural property and community. These localized hazards support
choosing a route that avoids Link F-20.
G. The Bartlett power line does not justify placing another major line on the same affected
community.
    Routing criteria may consider existing compatible rights-of-way, but the Bartlett power line
on or near Link F-20 should not automatically justify another major transmission facility in the
same affected area. The proper question is whether that choice remains reasonable after
considering community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, habitable
structures, safety, engineering feasibility, and cumulative impacts.
    The existence of one power line should not mean that the same landowners and community
resources must bear a second, larger, and more intrusive transmission burden without careful
review.
H. Link F-21 is preferable to Link F-20 if the ALJs compare the two links.

    If the ALJs compare F-20 and F-21, Ms. Randolph requests a finding that F-21 is less
harmful. Based on the local evidence, F-21 avoids or reduces the most serious harms associated
with F-20: proximity to the Howton residence and agricultural improvements, impacts near
Cedar Valley Church, Buttermilk Creek and Gault cultural-resource concerns, tornado-recovery



                                                3
 burdens, wildfire and vegetation concerns, cumulative impacts near the Bartlett power line, and
impacts to inhabited homes.
   Those differences support giving greater weight to F-21 over F-20 under PURA Section
37.056(c)(4) and the Commission's routing criteria.
I. Health, noise, visual, and quality-of-life concerns support giving weight to local evidence.

    Ms. Randolph is not offering medical expert testimony. Her testimony and concerns
regarding visual impacts, audible corona noise, reduced enjoyment and use of property, potential
effects on residents and livestock, and long-term property-value impacts are offered as local
landowner and family evidence.
    Those concerns should not be dismissed because Ms. Randolph is pro se or because her
interest is as Nelda Howton's daughter and future heir. The routing decision affects real homes,
land, livestock, churches, cultural resources, and rural community life.
J. Preferred Route 296 should be recommended instead of Route 894 or any route using
Link F-20.

    Ms. Randolph requests that the ALJs recommend Preferred Route 296. The decisive point is
that Link F-20 would cause concentrated and avoidable impacts to her family property, livestock
operations, storm-vulnerable land, cultural resources, and rural community.
   Route 296 is more direct and avoids the unnecessary harms associated with Link F-20. If the
Applicants and the Commission maintain that the proposed 765-kV line does not create health
concerns sufficient to reject a route, that position should not be applied selectively to reject
Route 296 while imposing the line closer to existing homes, agricultural operations, churches,
and cultural resources on Link F-20.
    If additional route findings are needed, Ms. Randolph requests a finding that any approved
route should avoid Link F-20 and minimize impacts to residences, agricultural operations,
community values, church and cultural resources, wildfire-prone vegetation, storm recovery,
environmental integrity, and established rural communities.
V. PROPOSED FINDINGS SUPPORTED BY MS. RANDOLPH'S TESTIMONY
1. Stacy Randolph is Nelda Howton's daughter, a pro se intervenor, and a future heir of the
   Howton property.
2. Her testimony is based on personal observations, family knowledge, and her expected future
    interest in the property.
3. Ms. Randolph opposes all proposed routes using Link F-20, including Route 894.
4. Ms. Randolph requests approval of Preferred Route 296 or another route that does not use
   Link F-20.
5. The Howton property is used as a homesite and for cattle, horses, poultry, gardening, hunting,
    and general agricultural operations.
6. The record shows proximity impacts to the Howton residence and improvements.




                                                4
 7. The record includes storm damage, tornado recovery, wildfire risk, vegetation conditions,
    livestock operations, and family use of the property.
8. Cedar Valley Church is a community meeting place, and Buttermilk Creek and the Gault
    archeological area raise cultural-resource concerns.
9. The Bartlett power line should not automatically justify another major transmission facility
    without review of cumulative impacts, safety, engineering feasibility, and community
   burden.
10. PURA Section 37.056(c)(4) supports giving weight to the evidence concerning community
    values, historical and aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.
11. Routes using Link F-20 would impose concentrated and avoidable impacts on the Howton
    family property and surrounding rural community.
12. If the ALJs compare Link F-20 and Link F-21, the local evidence supports finding that Link
    F-21 is less harmful than Link F-20.
13. Preferred Route 296 is the route Ms. Randolph requests the ALJs recommend to the
    Commission.

VI. PRAYER
    For these reasons, Intervenor Stacy Randolph respectfully requests that the Administrative
Law Judges recommend that the Commission reject Route 894 and any other route using Link
F-20. Ms. Randolph further requests that the ALJs recommend approval of Preferred Route 296,
or another route that avoids Link F-20 and better protects residences, agricultural operations,
community values, church and cultural resources, storm recovery, wildfire safety, aesthetic
values, and environmental integrity.
    In the alternative, if the ALJs consider a link-level comparison, Ms. Randolph requests a
finding that Link F-21 is preferable to Link F-20 because it avoids or reduces the concentrated
harms associated with Link F-20.
   Ms. Randolph requests all other relief to which she may be justly entitled.

Respectfully submitted,
